analysis.one_liner: Makes drug companies repay a share of federal research money behind their products.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced in June 2000 with one cosponsor, was sent to three House committees and died in subcommittee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required any company selling a drug, biologic, or genetic product built on federally funded research to pay the government back a slice of its profits each year, capped at 20% of annual profits and ending when the patent expires. A new board would calculate how much federal money went into each product's development. The money would go into a trust fund to finance a Medicare prescription drug benefit if Congress enacted one, or otherwise fund pharmaceutical research and comparative effectiveness studies.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who funded the research but currently receive nothing back when companies patent and profit from the results. Medicare beneficiaries would gain if a drug benefit were enacted, since fund money would help finance it, and the public would gain from federally funded research on how well competing drugs actually work.

how_it_helps.text: Every federal research agreement that could lead to a pharmaceutical, biologic, or genetic product would have to include a clause requiring annual repayments to the government from the resulting profits.
The repayment equals the product's profits multiplied by the share of its development supported by federal money, capped at 20% of any year's profits and ending when the initial patent expires.
Up to 2% of the fund would pay for FDA or NIH research comparing the effectiveness of competing drugs — information that could help doctors and patients choose cheaper treatments that work as well.

If Congress enacted a Medicare prescription drug benefit, the rest of the fund would help pay for it; if no benefit had been enacted, the remainder would go to NIH for pharmaceutical and genetic research.

analysis.who_pays: Drug and biotechnology companies selling products whose development relied on federal research support, which would owe up to 20% of their profits on those products each year until the patent runs out. They would also bear the cost of audits and calculations by the new Public Investment Recovery Board, which could reach profits of people who were not party to the original federal agreement.

drawbacks.text: The repayment could reduce the incentive for companies to develop drugs and biologics from federally funded discoveries, potentially slowing the pipeline that turns public research into medicines.

The board would have to calculate the federal share of research behind every covered product, including profits earned by parties not involved in the original federal agreement, an audit burden that could invite years of disputes over the numbers.

The fund's largest allowed use (20%) is NIH research, and the Medicare-drug-benefit trigger left most of the money's purpose contingent on another bill Congress had not passed, so the proposal did not directly lower anyone's drug prices on its own.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill tackles a real imbalance: the public pays for basic research, then companies patent the results and charge whatever the market bears. Repaying up to 20% of profits on federally supported products would return some of that value to taxpayers, with the cap and patent-expiration limits protecting the industry's core reward for innovation. The cost is uncertainty — a new multi-agency board sorting out how much of each product's development was federally funded could be slow and contentious, and the money would not reach consumers directly unless a Medicare drug benefit passed. Even granting those design flaws, the bill never got far enough for any of them to be tested.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in House committees — referred to three of them, then to two subcommittees — and no committee ever acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Capuano introduced the Public Investment Recovery Act of 2000 on June 21, 2000, joined by Rep. Stark as the bill's only cosponsor.
The Speaker referred it to three committees — Commerce, Science, and Ways and Means — splitting it across jurisdictions with no timeline for consideration.
In the following weeks it was referred to the Science Committee's Basic Research Subcommittee and the Commerce Committee's Health and Environment Subcommittee, and no further action was ever taken.
The 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001, with the bill never having received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmaceutical and biotechnology companies that profit from products built on federally funded research are better off: no repayment requirement was ever created, and taxpayers received nothing back from that research during this Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug companies profiting from public research

for.name: Rep. Michael E. Capuano
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.

for.name: Rep. Fortney (Pete) Stark
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's only cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on June 21, 2000, referred it to its Health and Environment Subcommittee, and never held a hearing or markup before the Congress ended.

against.name: House Science Committee and House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill under split referral; the Science Committee sent it to its Basic Research Subcommittee, and neither committee reported it out.

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and the sole cosponsor were Democrats, but the bill never drew enough support for any vote, so no partisan split on the merits was ever recorded.

industries.note: The bill would have taken up to 20% of annual profits from any drug or biologic whose development relied on federal research support, ending at patent expiry. Its interest ran against the bill's beneficiaries, since the money repaid would otherwise stay with the companies.

industries.industry: National Institutes of Health and medical research nonprofits
industries.note: Federal support counted toward the repayment formula included NIH funding and the federal share of nonprofit research, but the same institutions were also set to receive fund money for pharmaceutical research and comparative effectiveness studies. The bill's mechanism flowed through the agencies that conduct the research it targets.
